chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Bid-Ask Spread: What It Is Made Of

lessons.title: The Roll Model: Estimating Effective Spreads from Price Reversals

body.text: You do not need a single bid or ask quote to estimate a historical spread. You only need to notice that a price series which keeps bouncing between two nearby points, up, down, up, down, is quietly telling you how wide those two points are.

children.text: The Problem: Often You Only Have Trade Prices, Not Quotes

Everything in this chapter so far has assumed you can see the bid and the ask directly. Most historical data a retail quant researcher can actually get their hands on, NSE's daily bhavcopy files, closing prices pulled from screener.in, or a simple end-of-day OHLC series, does not include the bid-ask quote at all. It only has the price at which trades actually happened. And yet, even from a bare series of trade prices, it is possible to estimate what the average spread must have been, using an idea Richard Roll published in 1984 that remains one of the most quoted results in market microstructure.
Roll's Insight: The Spread Creates Negative Serial Covariance

markDefs.definition: The tendency of trade prices to alternate between the bid and the ask even when the underlying fair value has not moved at all, purely because consecutive trades are executed by different sides of the market. A trade at the ask followed by one at the bid looks, in the raw price series, exactly like a decline, even if nothing fundamental changed.

children.text: Roll's starting observation is that trades do not happen only at one fixed fair value. A buy order trades at the ask; a sell order trades at the bid. If fair value itself is not moving, but trades keep alternating between hitting the ask and hitting the bid, the observed price series will bounce back and forth around that fair value purely mechanically. This is the

, and it leaves a specific statistical fingerprint: a price increase is more likely to be followed by a price decrease, and vice versa, than plain randomness would predict. In statistical terms, consecutive price changes have negative serial covariance, and the size of that negative covariance turns out to be mathematically tied to the size of the spread that is causing it.

body.caption: Roll's implied spread estimator. Cov(ΔP_t, ΔP_t-1) is the covariance between consecutive price changes; the spread s is only defined when this covariance is negative, since the formula requires taking a square root of a positive number.

body.title: Working the Roll Formula
body.prompt: A researcher computes the covariance between consecutive daily price changes for a stock and finds Cov(ΔP_t, ΔP_t-1) = -0.04 (in rupees squared). Using Roll's formula, what implied spread, in rupees, does this covariance suggest? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: s = 2 × √(−(−0.04)) = 2 × √0.04 = 2 × 0.20 = ₹0.40. A negative serial covariance of −0.04 in consecutive price changes is consistent with an average effective spread of about ₹0.40 over the period measured, purely from how the price bounces between trades.

children.text: Assumptions and When the Model Breaks

Roll's model is elegant precisely because it needs so little data, and that same simplicity is where its assumptions come from. It assumes the spread stays constant over the sample period, that a trade is equally likely to be a buy or a sell at each point in time, and, most importantly, that consecutive price changes have no genuine information content driving them serially, only the mechanical bid-ask bounce. Real markets routinely violate that last assumption, especially around results season or a policy announcement, when price changes really are serially informative rather than purely mechanical noise. When that happens, the estimated covariance can come out positive instead of negative, and the formula then asks for the square root of a negative number, which has no real solution. In practice, this means Roll's estimator frequently returns an undefined result on exactly the periods a researcher might be most curious about.

body.caption: Roll's model: what it assumes vs what real NSE data often looks like
headers: Where It Commonly Breaks in Practice

cells: The true spread does not change across the sample window
Spreads widen around results season, policy days, and expiry, exactly as covered earlier in this chapter
Consecutive price changes reflect only bid-ask bounce, not real news
Trending or event-driven periods carry genuine serial information, producing positive rather than negative covariance
Buys and sells arrive independently of the recent trade history
Order flow often clusters, for example algorithmic execution splitting one large order into a sequence of same-direction trades

body.text: Do not treat an undefined Roll estimate as a bug to work around by force. A positive serial covariance is itself informative: it usually means the price series over that window was driven by genuine, serially correlated information, which is exactly the kind of period this course's later chapters on adverse selection care about most.

Roll's model is rarely used today as a precise, final spread estimate. Its enduring value is as a first, data-only pass at whether a market was quietly efficient and mechanically noisy, or genuinely information-driven, using nothing more than a series of trade prices that any researcher can pull from NSE bhavcopy data or a broker's historical API.

body.title: Reading a Positive Covariance
body.question: A researcher computes Cov(ΔP_t, ΔP_t-1) = +0.02 for a stock during its results week. What does Roll's model say about this result?
options: The implied spread is negative, meaning the market maker was paying traders
Roll's estimator is undefined here, which itself suggests genuine information was driving prices that week
The spread must be exactly zero
body.explanation: Roll's formula requires taking the square root of the negative of the covariance. With a positive covariance of +0.02, that means taking the square root of −0.02, which has no real solution. Rather than a computational error, this is a meaningful signal in its own right: a positive serial covariance during results week is consistent with genuine, information-driven price moves rather than pure bid-ask bounce.

points: Roll's model estimates the effective bid-ask spread purely from a series of trade prices, without needing any quote data
The core insight is that bid-ask bounce, trades alternating between the bid and the ask, creates negative serial covariance in consecutive price changes
The formula s = 2√(−Cov(ΔP_t, ΔP_t-1)) converts that negative covariance into an implied spread estimate
The model assumes a constant spread, no serial information effect, and independently arriving buy and sell orders, all of which real markets frequently violate
A positive serial covariance makes the estimator undefined, and should be read as evidence of genuine information-driven price moves rather than a computation error
Roll's model is most useful today as a quick, data-only diagnostic of whether a price series looks mechanically noisy or information-driven, not as a precise final spread estimate
